paras: For much of the twentieth century, the standard map of modern art had a single center. The story began in Paris, passed briefly through a few other European capitals and eventually crossed the Atlantic to New York. Artists elsewhere appeared in this story, if at all, as followers: talented, perhaps, but essentially provincial, receiving ideas that had been invented somewhere else. The painter Tarsila do Amaral is one of the most persuasive reasons to doubt that map.

Born in 1886 into a wealthy family in the interior of São Paulo state, Tarsila was trained first in Brazil and then in Europe, and in the early 1920s she studied in Paris with painters associated with Cubism. It would be easy, and for decades it was common, to describe her as their gifted student. Yet the paintings she produced after returning home are difficult to explain as imitations. She kept the geometric structure she had learned abroad and filled it with the vernacular colors of rural Brazil, with the plants, hills and small towns of the landscape she remembered, and later with figures that no European teacher would have painted. In the 1930s her paintings of factory workers would take her in yet another direction.

A persistent misconception places Tarsila at the center of the Modern Art Week, the festival of exhibitions, concerts and readings held in São Paulo in February 1922, the year of the centennial of Brazilian independence. She was not there. She was in Paris, and she joined the circle of modernist writers and painters in São Paulo only after she returned later that year. The misconception is revealing, however, because it shows how completely her work came to seem emblematic of what the week had promised: an art that would be modern and Brazilian at the same time.

Nowhere is that promise clearer than in Abaporu, which she painted in 1928 as a birthday gift for her husband, the writer Oswald de Andrade. A seated figure with a tiny head and a disproportionate foot sits beside a cactus under a sun that looks like a slice of fruit. The title comes from Tupi-Guarani words usually translated as the man who eats people, and the painting inspired a manifesto for a new movement that proposed, provocatively, that Brazilian culture should devour foreign influences rather than obey them. The image is strange, funny and syncretic, and it refuses every exotic stereotype that European audiences might have brought to it.

The reappraisal of her work outside Latin America has been slow. It was only in 2018 that a major exhibition devoted entirely to her opened in the United States, organized by the Art Institute of Chicago and the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Many visitors who had never heard her name found themselves in front of paintings that had been famous in Brazil for generations. The delay says less about Tarsila than about the map. If modern art had only one center, her paintings must be peripheral. If, instead, modernism was invented in several places at once, in conversation rather than in obedience, then she belongs not at the edge of the story but at one of its many centers.

Neither a copy of Paris nor a rejection of it, her work asks a question that art historians are still learning to answer: what happens to the history of art when we stop assuming where it takes place?

parts: Five years before the Modern Art Week, a young painter named Anita Malfatti opened an exhibition in São Paulo.
Her canvases, shaped by years of study in Germany and the United States, used bold color and distorted forms.
The response was fierce.
A well-known writer published a polemic in a major newspaper, attacking the paintings as a symptom of foreign madness.
The attack wounded Malfatti deeply.
Yet it also drew together a group of young writers and artists who rallied to her defense.
Several of them would organize the festival of 1922.
In that sense, a hostile review helped to create the movement it was meant to destroy.

items.situation: Make it periodic: "Tarsila changed the map of modern art. She was trained in Paris and returned to São Paulo."
tips: Trained in Paris and returned to São Paulo, Tarsila changed the map of modern art.
Put the participle clauses first and the main clause last.

items.situation: Use neither... nor: "Her work is not a copy of Europe. It is not a rejection of Europe."
tips: Her work is neither a copy of Europe nor a rejection of it.
Neither... nor, with the same grammatical form after each.

items.situation: Fix the parallelism: "The painting is strange, funny and it provokes people."
tips: The painting is strange, funny and provocative.
Three adjectives, not two adjectives and a clause.

items.situation: Use not... but: "She did not paint for Paris. She painted for Brazil."
tips: She painted not for Paris but for Brazil.
The two parts after not and but must match.

items.situation: Build a tricolon about yourself for an essay.
tips: Raised in Brazil, fluent in English and at home in museums, I...
Three parallel phrases, then the main clause.

tips: European audiences tended to exoticize Brazilian art.
One precise verb replaces a whole description.

listenings.text: Welcome to this room, which I have to admit is the one I argued hardest for. For a long time, when museums in this country showed Tarsila do Amaral at all, they presented her mainly as a student of French painters, as if her importance were something she had brought back from Paris in her luggage. I want you to look at these paintings differently. Notice how she takes the structure she learned in Europe, the clean geometry, the flattened space, and fills it with things no Parisian painter was looking at: the colors of houses in small Brazilian towns, cacti, palm trees, hills and figures from her own country. Now, you may have noticed that we did not put this room at the end of the exhibition, after the Europeans, as a kind of postscript. We put her here, in the middle. That choice is an argument. It suggests that modern art did not have one center that everyone else copied. It had several, and they were talking to each other.

Let's talk about a week that is famous in Brazil and almost unknown in American textbooks. In February 1922, at the Municipal Theater in São Paulo, a group of young writers, musicians and painters organized what they called a Modern Art Week. It was the year of the centennial of Brazilian independence, and the timing was not an accident. The events were chaotic. Some concerts were interrupted by booing, some lectures were mocked, and many people in the audience clearly thought the whole thing was a joke. Now, here is a detail that surprises many students, including Brazilian ones. Tarsila do Amaral, who is now the painter most associated with Brazilian modernism, was not there. She was in Paris, and she joined the group only after she returned later that year. So why did the week matter, if it was so disorganized? Because it announced, publicly and very noisily, that Brazilian artists intended to be modern on their own terms, and not only as followers of Europe.
